Editorial

Rachel Acheson

Rachel Acheson

London, UK
rachel.acheson117@gmail.com

Rachel Acheson  

One of the great pleasures of being a Journal Editor is watching, and being part of, the journey an author goes on as they write and publish a paper. Often, you are only there for the last part – submission and publication – but occasionally, as is the case for me with a number of the papers in this issue, you are afforded glimpses along the way, which makes the enjoyment of the final stages all the greater. There is no doubt that the papers we publish take a great deal of work, often over long periods of time, and that as well as bringing pleasure, the writing process can be full of doubt, frustration, and requires a great deal of patience. However, in an age where quality journalism is on the decline, and ‘click bait’ online articles and fake news proliferate, the serious amount of time and thought that goes into professional writing is something to be valued, and, I believe, protected. Something I took from my predecessor Alexandra de Rementeria in this respect, and which parallels clinical work, is that it is often better to slow down and allow yourself to feel stuck, as what can emerge from this will be worth the pain it has cost you.

As we at the Journal and the ACP think about how to support members to write about their work, I have cause to reflect on the writing process. Why do clinicians feel motivated to write for publication? What helps this process, and what gets in the way? How do we, as a profession, foster a ‘facilitating environment’ for writers, thus ensuring we remain connected to each other, our history, and look to the future? I am interested to hear from any of our readers who have ideas about how the Journal and the ACP can support members in this respect. Please do get in touch if you have thoughts on this subject that you would like to share.

The authors of the first three papers in this issue take part of their inspiration from literature and myth – the Dickens novel ‘Bleak House’, the Greek myth of Pandora, and the Cornish folktale ‘A Tinners’ Rabbits Tale’. They remind me of the fact that when we work as psychoanalytic therapists, we bring the whole of who we are to the relationship with our patients, with our free associations reflecting what our mind has available to make sense of what it is encountering. While it is personal, art, in whatever form, allows the communication to reverberate. As Balfour aptly observes ‘the longevity of folktales lies in our ability to make them our own – that they might move beyond their subjective origin’ and signals her hope that ‘there remains space for you the reader, to recognise and translate into your own experience aspects of the tale and thus take possession of the story for yourselves’.

A Tinners’ Rabbits Tale: A Contemporary Cornish Folktale. Story, Story-Making and Storytelling. A Narration of the Emergence of Story from a Clinical Encounter

Laura D. C. Balfour

Laura D. C. Balfour

UK
laura.balfour@nhs.net

Laura D. C. Balfour   ACP member working as a consultant child psychotherapist in the NHS in Cornwall, and as a visiting lecturer at the Tavistock Clinic in London. Sol Andreson is a freelance illustrator working in Cornwall and graduate of the University of Falmouth.
Folktale, child psychotherapy, Tinners’ Rabbits, metamorphosis

‘A Tinners’ Rabbits Tale’ is a contemporary folktale, which draws upon Cornish traditions of storytelling. The story grew from a clinical encounter and draws upon the mysterious and archaic symbol of the ‘Tinners’ Rabbits’ - three rabbits (or hares) forming a circle by connection at the ear. The reflective commentary which accompanies it explores the development of the story from a therapeutic encounter and describes how it became a vehicle for the uncovering of unconscious feeling in the therapist and dynamics within the relationship, facilitating development within the clinical encounter itself. The story and reflective commentary explore the working of boundaries between self and other, reality and fantasy, with particular attention to the idea of metamorphosis and how change can be both provoked and inspired. Story, story-making and storytelling are considered, alongside the importance of inspiration, provocation, and impact.

Therapists’ Questions in Short Term Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy with Depressed Adolescents

Alice Dehl , Elizabeth Edginton and Nick Midgley

Nick Midgley

London, UK
alice.dehl@gmail.com

London, UK
http://orcid.org/0000-0002-6263-5058

Oxford, UK

Nick Midgley   Child and adolescent psychotherapist, and Professor of Psychological Therapies with Children and Young People at Anna Freud/UCL. He has co-written and edited various books, including Therapeutic Work for Children with Complex Trauma: A Three-Track Psychodynamic Approach (Routledge, 2023), Essential Research Findings in Child and Adolescent Counselling and Psychotherapy (Sage, 2017), Mentalization-Based Treatment for Children: A Time-Limited Approach (APA, 2017) and Short-term Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy for Adolescents with Depression (Karnac, 2016).
Depression, adolescence, negative transference, STPP

Questions are an integral part of therapeutic exchanges, but little empirical work has been done on how questions are used within psychoanalytic psychotherapy sessions. This study explores how therapists use questions in short term psychoanalytic psychotherapy (STPP) sessions with depressed adolescents. Three STPP cases were selected and questions asked by the therapist were identified, transcribed, and analysed in terms of type and function. A specific type of question (considered as ‘performative’) was noted as being of interest. These questions and the patients’ responses were analysed using Conversation Analysis (CA). A high number of questions were asked across all cases, with type and function generally comparable to findings from non-therapeutic conversational settings. The specific questions identified as ‘performative’ were used by therapists to verbalise patients’ unspoken negative thoughts and feelings towards them. A high proportion of avoidant responses to these questions was found. These results have consequences for refining clinical technique and the training of psychotherapists undertaking STPP with depressed adolescents, with particular reference to addressing the negative transference.

Infant Observation During Lockdown: The Screen as Psychic Portal

Maeve McIlwain

Maeve McIlwain

London, UK
maevemcilwain@gmail.com

Maeve McIlwain   Third year trainee at the Tavistock, working across the fostering, adoption and kinship care team and a community perinatal service. Maeve’s doctoral research is on the experience of LGBTQ clinicians in the consulting room, and their pre-clinical masters thesis was about the symbolic function of learning tasks in work with psychotic adolescents in a school on an in-patient unit.
Infant observation, screens, Interdependency, loss, neutrality

This paper discusses the author’s experience of conducting an infant observation via video call during the pandemic. Using vignettes, the author explores how a screen-based format challenged traditional understanding of infant observation, necessitating a rethinking of technique and theory. The author argues that this was a productive disturbance, requiring useful reconsideration of the task and how we think about observation, perspective, participation and neutrality. This is held alongside the developing context of the pandemic, and how these extraordinary conditions – seen through the prism of the developing infant – sharpened psychoanalytic concerns of dependency, separateness, desire and loss. The author considers some of the ways the pandemic continues to have consequences in our world today, and how it might relate to our work. Some possible clinical implications regarding online sessions are formulated, as well as the psychoanalytic function of these technologies in the psyche.

Response to the 2024 ACP Annual Conference ‘Inside Digital Lives: Growing Up in the Information Age’: Decoding the Algorithm of the Digital World

Pippa Watson

Pippa Watson

contact@pippawatsonpsychotherapy.com

Pippa Watson  

I attended the ACP conference in June 2024 in the final months of my child psychotherapy training. I rarely had time for additional lectures or conferences, let alone a whole weekend. However, the conference on the impact of digital technologies on child development was an exception, as I believe this topic is not only vital to my child psychotherapy practice but also to the future of humanity. The conference discussions were heavy, evoking fear and despair, yet I found myself leaning towards a more optimistic perspective. It could very well be that the conference felt too threatening and therefore evoked a need to deny the awfulness of it all. It could also be a defence, since I am a Millennial and a social media user. My age places me in a unique position, bridging generations with differing relationships to technology, which might shape my ability to both empathise with younger clients and critically reflect on the digital landscape. Yet I am not a digital native and grew up knocking on my friends’ doors to go play outside. Nevertheless, as an individual, I am often drawn to think existentially and about how ‘the collective unconscious’- a concept introduced by Carl Jung (1936), referring to a deeper layer of the unconscious which is not individual but universal among all people- shapes the day-to-day thoughts, feelings and behaviours of my young patients and vice versa. It is through this lens that I write this response piece. I will first highlight the key insights from the conference regarding child development and then explore how the use of digital technology, though arguably regressive, may be part of a ‘cultural complex’- a post-Jungian concept as discussed by Singer (2010), which I will elaborate on later- paving the way for a transcendence of the collective psyche.

Professor Lemma’s compelling paper (Lemma, 2021), which explored the impact of widespread use of online pornography, opened the conference, and a door to the digital world. Research findings presented exemplified the scale of the problem, including its links to sexual violence, layering shock and horror at every turn of the paper. It felt like falling off a cliff right down to the deep, dark web; the scariest corners of which pervert our ‘internal worlds’. She reported that pornography websites received more visitors than Netflix, Amazon and Twitter combined (Wright, Tokunaga & Herbenick, 2023) and that 60-80% of adult men and 37% of women say they use pornography on a regular basis (Ballester-Arnal et al., 2023). Within the first ten minutes of the presentation I was gripped because this felt personal. What I was learning was not just an issue relevant to my work, but to the majority of the population. The problems discussed, including the dehumanisation that pornography can cause, leading to the normalisation of sexual violence, penetrated me with fear and an intense desire to protect my patients from these harms. This was Lemma’s intention in bringing the material to the conference, and rightly so. We cannot allow these digital ravines to erode into deep canyons of disconnection in society. From this first paper, a tone of fear and indignation was set for me for the rest of the conference.

James Joyce and the Internal World of the Replacement Child, by Mary Adams, London and New York, Routledge, 2024, 144 pp., £18.99 (paperback), ISBN 9781032314778

Christopher Long

Christopher Long

Coventry, UK
chrislong365@yahoo.com

Christopher Long  

In the foreword to her book ‘James Joyce and the internal world of the replacement child’, Mary Adams tells us of her own grief at the death of her husband James Fisher, which interrupted their plans to collaborate using his writing on the imagination and clinical material from Mary’s patients. In her bereavement, she turned to the work of James Joyce, and in particular ‘Ulysses’ where she found themes of loss and grief that resonated and gave shape to her own experience. She also noted that other themes in the work such as guilt, abandonment, fear of condemnation, punishment and a sense of claustrophobia were also present in the material her ‘replacement child’ patients brought to her. Adams uses the term ‘replacement child’ to describe either those born into a family mourning the loss of an older sibling or those who experience the death of a sibling within the family at a young age.

It seems from the many descriptions of him by his friends and acquaintances that Joyce’s soul was restless and tortured for much of his life. Adams points to the themes of self-condemnation, isolation and anger to be found within his work. She describes something like a grieving process that can be traced through ‘Portrait of the artist as a young man’, ‘Ulysses’ and ‘Finnegans wake’; a grief for lost objects and a lost home in the form of Dublin and Ireland from which Joyce exiled himself. Despite this self-imposed exile, Joyce never stopped writing about Dublin, as if the only possible way to understand it was to extricate himself and view it apart and at a distance. Adams explores the self-banishment of the replacement child as seen in her patients as an alienation from family and belonging and which is also expressed in Joyce’s writing and in his self-exile from his beloved Ireland.

Adams maintains that through his writing Joyce comes to find a way of processing his own emotional experience, creating some space between himself and it, before it can be understood and properly claimed back as a tolerable part of the self. Just as a patient might use their analyst’s mind, Joyce uses the page to work through the material and we can trace how it changes over time becoming freer, more poetic and dreamlike by the time he is writing ‘Finnegans wake’.

Marion Milner: A Contemporary Introduction, by Alberto Stefana and Alessio Gamba, London, Routledge, 2024, London, 132 pp., £14.99 (paperback), ISBN 9781003330332

Paola Silvia Ferri

Paola Silvia Ferri

paolasilvia.ferri@gmail.com

Paola Silvia Ferri  

This fascinating book by Alberto Stefana and Alessio Gamba introduces us to an important and relatively overlooked psychoanalyst, despite her creative contributions to psychoanalysis and the revolutionary thinking of Donald Winnicott.

Marion Milner, who lived to the grand age of 98 (1900–1998), belonged to the British Independent Group and began her training at the British Society in 1940. After an initial Jungian analysis, she came to Winnicott following a period of analysis with Sylvia Payne, who she left after four years. This was on the advice of Clifford Scott, her future analyst, who had already analysed Winnicott’s two wives. Winnicott was the supervisor of ‘Susan’, Milner’s patient who is introduced in this book by Stefana and Gamba in the last two chapters, and who Winnicott himself invited to stay in his house, which he sometimes did with difficult patients (Milner, 1969/2010).

Milner, Winnicott and other psychoanalysts, including Bion, Klein, and Meltzer were part of a group of intellectuals (the Imago group), who met regularly to talk about music, poetry and free thoughts. They were close to the Bloomsbury group, including Virginia Woolf and friends, and linked to the thinking of British Empiricism. Milner’s approach to psychoanalysis would today be considered as experimental.

The premise of this book is found in the concept of the ‘oceanic feeling’ that Freud describes in ‘Civilization and its discontents’ (1929): Freud speaks about it as akin to primary narcissism, typical of the newborn child, which has to be tolerated and shared; it is an experience of non-differentiation, which the mystic Rolland calls the ‘oceanic feeling’, a fusion with the world, a sense of belonging and universal sharing, which is the basis of our existence. We are talking about the first fundamental experience, a necessary premise for the definition of one’s separateness. Thus, for psychoanalysts, the first experience with the mother-environment is central: if we did not have a ‘good enough’ mother (Winnicott, 1958), our capacity for separateness, for a definition of autonomous identity, will be not favoured. The child must therefore be able to experience its own omnipotence, the feeling of not having a limit and of being able to use the world around him/her, through the maternal object.

Witches (Elizabeth Sankey, 2024): An Exploration of Motherhood and Mental Health

Iva Ajder

Iva Ajder

UK
iajder@tavi-port.nhs.uk

Iva Ajder   Tavistock trained Child & Adolescent Psychoanalytic Psychotherapist. She works in the NHS and in private practice.

At the London Film Festival this year, a striking number of films tackled the theme of motherhood, a reflection of both artistic focus and broader societal concerns. Many of these films, including ‘Witches’, were directed by women, marking a festival notably shaped by female voices. With 44% of films directed by female and non-binary filmmakers, the festival’s line-up sheds light on topics like postnatal depression, psychosis, and the societal expectations placed on mothers. An article in The Guardian about the film festival, aptly titled ‘Maternity in the spotlight’ (Kohmami, 2024) captures this collective turn towards exploring the depths and challenges of motherhood.

Beyond the festival, ‘Witches’ arrives at a time when the UK’s maternal health services are under scrutiny for failing to support new and expectant mothers adequately. Reports from the Care Quality Commission (2024) reveal ongoing gaps in care, especially for mothers from minority backgrounds, reflecting systemic neglect that is painfully relevant to ‘Witches’’ story. The film addresses not only personal but also societal blind spots in maternal care.

Idealised Motherhood

Directed by Elizabeth Sankey, ‘Witches’ offers a powerful portrayal of postpartum depression and psychosis through the lens of a new mother. Sankey uses personal narration alongside clips from classic films, weaving together an idealised, almost mythical image of motherhood. Images of dream-like mothers and babies fill the screen; an idealised phantasy world where new mothers go from ‘strength to strength’, are ‘glowing, feeling overjoyed and complete’, an image of endless emotional and physical resources. In these scenes, mothers appear serene and self-possessed, embodying a ‘good witch’ archetype like Glinda in ‘The Wizard of Oz’. The grainy footage of films from the sixties and seventies creates a soft, warm and nostalgic visual atmosphere, adding to the sweet, heavenly feeling portrayed in films about motherhood.

The gentle visuals begin to feel almost claustrophobic and one starts to feel uneasy as Sankey subtly hints at the painful disconnect between the ideal and many women’s lived reality. This idealisation might function as a defence against the deeper, more unsettling aspects of motherhood, denying the ambivalence and psychic strain that accompany the role. As viewers are pulled between these two polarities, Sankey invites us to consider the impossible ‘ego ideal’ imposed on mothers (Freud, 1923).

Research Digest: Psychological Interventions Via Telephone and Internet Revisited

Helen Ritzema

Helen Ritzema

helen.ritzema@childpsychotherapy.org.uk

Helen Ritzema  

The topic of psychological interventions via telephone and internet (also termed teletherapy, videotherapy) was last investigated within the Research Digest in April 2020 at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. Within this Research Digest, the papers presented included published research, looking into: internet-based psychodynamic psychotherapy for adolescents experiencing depression (Lindqvist et al., 2020), experiences of Singaporean primary school children accessing counselling via a live chat portal (Kit et al., 2019), a group videoconferencing intervention for parents of children with a life-threatening illness (Rayner et al., 2016), and clinicians’ experiences of using remote technology to deliver therapy (Cipolletta & Mocellin, 2018; Trub & Magaldi, 2017). Articles were also presented which looked at developing and or training clinicians to offer remote therapeutic interventions for people living in rural areas, with little access to therapeutic services (Duncan et al. 2014; McCord et al. 2015). The Research Digest also included papers which covered theoretical ideas and observations on offering psychoanalysis via videoconference (Gutiérrez, 2017), reviews of the literature (Perle & Nierenberg, 2013), and a review of studies comparing telephone and face-to-face therapy (Irvine et al., 2020).

Since then, a vast number of papers looking at the impact of online working have been published within the JCP, the majority of which have focused on the impact of moving from face to face/in person therapeutic interactions to online/remote settings from a psychoanalytic perspective. Many of these papers were published in the special edition of the JCP, ‘Child psychotherapy in the time of Covid: voices from around the world on working through a pandemic’, issued in December 2020 (Holloway et al. 2020; Zuppardi, 2020; Carpi Lapi et al. 2020; Zaharia & Anagnostaki, 2020; Hutchison, 2020; Paiva, 2020; Neven, 2020; Shulman, 2020; Hart, 2020; Cohen, 2020; Sloan Donachy, 2020; Acquarone, 2022). Within the special edition, Pozzi Monzon and Micotti (2020) provided a literature review on digital psychoanalytic psychotherapy with children, adolescents and families. Included in their title was the statement ‘making the best of a bad job’. This appeared to suggest that working digitally with children, adolescents and families equates to a ‘bad job’. It is noted that, with some level of scepticism, Pozzi, Monzon and Micotti, write within their conclusion that ‘It seems that there is unanimous acceptance that different technological devices can, despite their limitations, lead to therapeutic results’ (2020, p. 278).

Editorial

Rachel Acheson

Rachel Acheson

London, UK
rachel.acheson117@gmail.com

Rachel Acheson  

In my last editorial, I wrote about the pleasure I take in my role at the Journal in seeing papers develop, sometimes over extended periods of time. The papers in this issue have reminded me how much I enjoy the fact that being part of the Journal has necessitated me spending a lot of time reading, which I otherwise might have considered a luxury. What we publish in the Journal is very varied, and while we occasionally run themed issues, there is often little to obviously connect papers other than their relevance to child and adolescent psychoanalytic psychotherapy. However, in the many hours spent preparing each issue, and in the discussions with my fellow Journal editors Lucy Mills and Krisna Catsaras, threads of connection can emerge which highlight aspects of concern or development within our profession.

In this issue, my fellow editors and I have been struck by the importance and respect the authors give to the consciously articulated narrative of their patients, even when this is starkly at odds with their understanding of the unconscious communications. Balancing the patient’s sense of ‘truth’ alongside the underlying story of their symptoms, and bringing these two more closely together, is in many ways the ‘bread and butter’ of our work. However, this balance has not always been well achieved in our clinical writing. This is partly about tone, but also the therapeutic attitude that comes across in the writing. While ethical publishing continues to be an issue that we grapple with, I remain optimistic that the way our profession is developing its writing style will allow us to continue to share our work without doing harm to our patients.

Another interesting aspect of this issue is that it contains three research papers and a clinical/theoretical paper, which has emanated from a piece of research, which is more than we tend to have. This fact only occurred to me in preparing this editorial, and came as something of a surprise, I think because of how clinically rich I find these papers. Credit goes to our authors for writing in a way that privileges the clinical implications of the research they have conducted, which I imagine is part of their motivation to publish. I hope these papers feel accessible to members of our profession who did not have research as part of their training, and that we can continue to publish research written up in this way.

Lida Anagnostaki MSc. PHD and Alexandra Zaharia MD

Alexandra Zaharia

Athens, Greece
lanagnostaki@ecd.uoa.gr

Cholargos, Greece

Alexandra Zaharia   Child and adolescent psychiatrist and psychoanalytic psychotherapist. She is full member and member of the Board of Supervisors of the Hellenic Association of Child and Adolescent Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy. Her research interests include early parent-child separation, psychoanalysis and politics, and the setting in psychoanalytic psychotherapy.
Institutional transference, transference, unaccompanied minors, refugees, idealisation, trauma

This study explores institutional transference towards institutions for children affected by war, a hitherto unexplored form of institutional transference for this age group. It focuses on adults who, as children during or right after the Greek Civil War, were placed in paidopoleis, i.e. institutions for war-struck children. The aim is to draw parallels to gain a deeper understanding of children in a similar position today, particularly unaccompanied refugee children, and to inform therapeutic work with this population. The themes that emerged from the analysis of the data demonstrated that the participants had established powerful institutional transferences, which had largely shaped their relationships both inside and outside the institution, as well as their identities. The clinical implications of these findings are discussed.

Adolescent motherhood, mothering, childhood relationships, grandmothers, Family Nurse Partnership, psychoanalytic research

This paper describes the writer’s experience of carrying out doctoral research exploring links between childhood relationships and adolescent motherhood. It presents some of the findings from the study - ‘What can young mothers’ accounts of their childhood relationships tell us about why they become parents? An Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis study of mothers aged 16–19 supported by the Family Nurse Partnership’, which was conducted through a psychoanalytic lens. Some of the relational dynamics uncovered in the young mothers’ accounts were unanticipated and striking, and may help clinically with understanding adolescent psychotherapy patients’ losses and longings. These include the absolute dominance of adolescent mothers’ mothers (extending even to maternal grandmothers and great-grandmothers) in the interview data, participants’ excessive experiences of being projected into, and the psychic difficulties caused by a fragile relationship between their parents.

Investigating Dissatisfied Dropout from Short Term Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy for Adolescents with Depression: A Single-Case Study

Nick Elsey and Evrinomy Avdi

Evrinomy Avdi

London, UK
Nicholas.elsey.18@ucl.ac.uk

Thessaloniki, Greece

Evrinomy Avdi   Professor of Clinical Psychology at the School of Psychology, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Greece, and Research Tutor at the Anna Freud National Centre for Children and Families, London. She is director of the Laboratory of Applied Psychology, Aristotle University, where she conducts research, works clinically and provides clinical supervision. Her main research interests concern psychotherapy research; she uses qualitative approaches to study therapy process, primarily using discursive, dialogical and narrative analytic methods in conjunction with analysing nonverbal interaction and physiological activation.
Adolescence, dropout, discourse analysis, STPP, case study, psychoanalytic psychotherapy

Dropout from therapy is a significant concern for providers of adolescent psychotherapy due to the potential impact on resources and outcomes. Some of those who drop out do so as they are dissatisfied with their treatment, however there is little research into the therapeutic processes that precede dissatisfied dropout. This single case study aims to further our understanding of the interactional processes that are implicated in psychoanalytic therapy, where the client dropped out and remained dissatisfied with their treatment. The research material consisted of audio-recordings of sessions from one case of Short Term Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy (STPP) from the IMPACT study, a randomised controlled trial of psychotherapy for adolescents with depression. The therapy was selected from a sample of ‘dissatisfied dropouts’, that had been identified in a previous study of participants who stopped therapy as they did not feel it was helpful. The therapy was with a female who dropped out of therapy after eight sessions and was deemed to have been ‘dissatisfied’ with her treatment. Three sessions were selected for analysis, drawn from the beginning, middle and end phases of treatment. The sessions were transcribed verbatim and analysed using discourse analysis. The findings identified specific actions the therapist took to attempt to construct the young person’s problem as psychological in nature, which the young person most often rejected. Over the course of therapy, the young person’s responses shifted from implicitly rejecting the therapist’s interventions to explicitly rejecting them. The findings suggest that initial rejection of the therapist’s construction of the ‘problem’ may be an indicator of upcoming dissatisfied dropout and suggestions for further research include investigating whether such dissatisfied dropouts can be reduced through adaptation of technique.

Fung Ko   Registered play therapist in private practice with a special interest in childhood autism, and she is a candidate with the China Study Group of the International Psychoanalytical Association. With three decades of experience marketing products containing addictive ingredients like caffeine and nicotine, she has transformed her interest in human behaviour into a deep passion for psychoanalysis. After earning her BBA and MBA in Hong Kong, she pursued academic psychology part-time, ultimately obtaining both a bachelor’s and a master’s degree. In 2018, Ko received her PhD from the University of Essex under the supervision of Professor R. D. Hinshelwood. Her research centred on the relationship between addiction and psychoanalytic concepts, with a particular focus on Winnicott’s theories of the mother-infant relationship and transitional objects. She explored how cigarettes may function as regressed forms of transitional objects in adulthood. In 2024, Ko published her PhD thesis as a book titled A psychoanalytic approach to smoking cessation: the cigarette as a transitional object, with Professor Hinshelwood as her background advisor.
Autism spectrum disorder/ASD, psychoanalytically informed play therapy, outcome research, PRISMA

Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is an extremely complex, heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder, which is linked to an ever-growing number of genes and multiple biological mechanisms. Converging evidence suggests that effective psychotherapy can reduce perceived early relational deprivation and stimulate adaptive neuroplasticity to ameliorate ASD. This paper aims to track the emotional development of a six-year-old child diagnosed with mild ASD in Hong Kong during a six-month weekly psychoanalytic psychotherapy single case study. The Protocol for Psychoanalytic Investigation of Signs Mapping Changes in Autism (PRISMA) is used as an assessment instrument. Psychoanalytic theory of ASD proposed by Frances Tustin is the primary theoretical framework supporting this research. It postulates that autistic behaviours are an attempt to deal with the unbearable catastrophic existential anxiety arising out of the child’s premature awareness of bodily separation from the feeding mother. Results suggest that all the scores across the six PRISMA categories, including sense of interest in people or objects, shared interactions, sensory integration, constitution of internal space, symbolic capacity, and transference field, improved over the treatment period. The PRISMA score progression suggests that psychoanalytic psychotherapy promotes psychic and emotional development and hence could be considered as one of the therapy modalities of choice for ASD. Additionally, current research demonstrates how objective and quantitative methods can be used to track the more subjective process of therapy. A replication of the study across a wider patient population could help improve generalisability.

In the last 15 years, the public mental health sector has been subject to two big policy shifts that have impacted the ability of Community Mental Health Teams (CMHTs) and Specialist Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service (CAMHS) clinics to deliver therapeutic services. This paper discusses the impact of the Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) policy and the Health and Social Care Act (2012) on these services and the various barriers to effective treatment that they have created. The author then proposes that, as psychoanalytic psychotherapists, with our particular awareness of unconscious and group processes, we are well-placed to support multidisciplinary colleagues in overcoming feelings of hopelessness, anxiety and impotence that these policy shifts create and takes inspiration from potentially analogous situations with patients as a method to approaching the systemic aspects of our work.

Andrew Briggs   Trained at the Tavistock as a child psychotherapist in the early 1990s and then as an organisational consultant in the 2000s. He supervises clinicians, and lectures and teaches on the application of Bion’s thinking to organisational problems and the practitioner’s capacity to think about reality and truth. After reading James Norris’s article ‘(Overcoming) attacks on thinking: the importance of psychoanalytic thinking in surviving systemic fragmentation of the public health sector’ I felt compelled to respond with thoughts that I have held for some years. These concern the question – why does our profession remain in CAMHS? After all, it is an environment inconducive to our way of experiencing and thinking about the subjectivity of patients, their families, and the work-team environment. In the 18 years until my retirement in 2018, I was head of child psychotherapy within various large NHS Trusts, a position that gave me a seat in the Trusts’ senior management teams. These years saw my informal job description require me to be squashed between the demands of clinicians and the policy directives of Trust boards. The upside was that I learned a great deal about how the implementation of service contracts was experienced by all levels of management and clinicians. Since retirement I have been contracted as an external consultant to many mental health teams due to their staff’s low morale. Norris highlights low morale as one consequence of the removal of the need for clinicians to understand complexity in patients. He sees this removal as made almost explicit in mental health policies that have created the NICE underwritten IAPT service delivery model. Norris sees them as an attack on psychoanalytic thinking. Whilst he offers a plausible psychoanalysis of how these attacks are motivated and targeted, I do not think he gives a complete picture. This is because he locates the only origin of the attacks as outside the psychoanalytic disciplines. In being split in this way, this picture cannot be the full reality. Attacks go on within each of the mental health disciplines. Colleagues, including child psychotherapists, are rivalrous and some find their envy destructive. Then, there are the perennial rivalries between disciplines, usually motivated by the desire to acquire more prestige and posts than others within their clinic’s multi-disciplinary team. However, the attacks I am more concerned about here are those we each use, individually and collectively, on our capacity to think.

James Norris’ paper invites us to consider not only the structural disintegration of NHS mental health services, but also the psychic fragmentation this engenders in those who work within them. In drawing on psychoanalytic frameworks, Norris illuminates the attacks on thinking that emerge when organisations become saturated with anxiety, loss and unprocessed grievances. I want to respond to this by building on his reflections in exploring how unconscious processes might manifest in Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS), where the weight of these dynamics are acutely felt.

Norris’ paper is well written and well researched. The focus initially is on the negative impact of recent changes in the long history of the undermining and fragmentation of the NHS. He mentions two major policy shifts resulting in IAPT (Improving Access to Psychological Therapies) and the Health and Social Care Act, their negative impact on services and the blocks to treatment they have created.

The NHS has long functioned not just as a healthcare provider but symbolising care, dependability and the containing function of the benign state. Its creation was fraught with conflict: political, economic and ideological. The early resistance from the British Medical Association and the Conservative Party reflects a deeper ambivalence about dependency, socialism and the loss of power.

Letwin and Redwood’s (1988) blueprint for privatisation can be read as a defence against vulnerability – an attempt to replace a containing structure with the promise of market profitability. As privatisation advances in stealth, the NHS shifts from being a predictable, unified, ubiquitous service to a network of fragmented services often in competition with each other. This has a profound effect on those working within the organisation and leads to mistrust, anxiety and splitting.

The private sector, particularly the health insurance companies from the US who have more or less saturated their own country now see a huge potential pot of money to exploit in the UK, and in fact, before the Shard at London Bridge was even built, US health insurance companies had reserved floors for their offices. US insurance companies have got their tentacles in so many things in our NHS, like services for scans, pathology and ultrasounds. Even NHS 111 is not run by the NHS.

Danny Goldberger  

In May 2020, Lyndsey Stonebridge wrote in ‘The New Statesman’:

What if instead of seeing the NHS as a frail but plucky thing that needs protecting, we thought of it instead as the table around which we all need to get to create a really different – and possibly more human – political future? What if getting back to work might also be a way of getting back to the human condition?

Stonebridge was writing as the nation was returning to work following one of the Covid-19 lockdowns. Here, there is a suggestion that we frame the NHS in more realistic terms and not as simply showing its worth in times of crisis, as happened with Covid-19, but as a functioning service with intention and purpose. In this commentary, I want to provide some examples of this intentionality in working as psychoanalytic child and adolescent psychotherapists in the NHS.

One of the arguments Stonebridge (2020) makes is that the philosopher Hannah Arendt’s distinction between ‘work’ and ‘labour’ might guide our attempts to build a better society. In relation to Norris’s outline, I am thinking about Arendt’s distinction in these ways, as conceptualised in her book ‘The Human Condition’ (Arendt, 1958). She suggests that ‘labour’ is thought of as those activities that are borne out of biological necessity, often cyclical and repetitive. ‘Work’ is more about the outcome, the world of things, perhaps linear or even goal-oriented and with the intention of achieving ends. Stonebridge (2020) stated that ‘work … gives collective meaning to what we do.’ ‘Action’ is connected to new beginnings and having a role in shaping the public sphere – a more revolutionary aim that is likely beyond the scope of this commentary but is made more possible in the way that we engage with the current system and its restrictions within the NHS.

Using this political and philosophical formulation, ‘labour’ will include those activities that denude meaning if they overtake the entirety of tasks, such as the increasing burden of documentation, outcome monitoring and crisis management pushing out other clinical work. ‘Work’ is seen in the development of durable systems such as care pathways, strategic plans and involvement in policy development.

Peter Blake  

This book is a real gem – it is musical in both senses of the word. It continues the work of Graham Music and takes us back to literally the very beginning of life; the hidden world of the womb. Music’s previous publications, which are always written in a very personable and accessible style, have introduced readers to the complexity and interaction of the forces of nature and nurture. This is evident in this most recent publication. He presents the very difficult area of neurological and biological functioning in a way that even I, someone who finds it nearly impossible to hold on to any Latin term, can understand.

More than any other book I have read, Womb life takes the reader on a tour of the gestation of a human being. While psychoanalytic authors such as Klein, Bion, Winnicott, Tustin and Meltzer discuss the earliest formation of the self, of the development of a me and not-me, Music takes us back even further to our very cellular beginnings. I used to think Klein’s work highlighted the bedrock of the formation of our personality, but this wonderful publication, along with earlier offerings by authors such as Liley (1972) and Piontelli (1992), make us reassess the origins of the psyche. It reminded me of Bion’s (2005) comments about when is a person born. Why do we date this to a biological birth? Are some of us born before our physical birth and arrive with great psychic sensitivity, while for others it may take several weeks or months to arrive at such a state?

This book has important implications for psychotherapy with children, adolescents and adults. The pre-natal history of the people we see must be taken very seriously. Practically, this means taking a greater interest in the details of the conception and pregnancy in our history taking – obviously easier to do with the parents of small children than with adolescents or adults. Also, this early exploration must be undertaken with great sensitivity and timing to avoid any sense of persecuting the biological mother. While reading the book I was reminded of a recent case of domestic violence I supervised in which the pregnant mother was physically assaulted, with direct violence towards the womb. I wondered what impact this could have had on the foetus and now on the child who was being presented. Interestingly, the child was referred for violent physical outbursts and this publication made me think much more about this link.

‘Forensic psychoanalysis’ is the latest addition to a long list of hugely engaging books by Professor Brett Kahr, a prominent academic historian and psychoanalyst. Each chapter weaves a rich tapestry of thinking about criminality with exceptional attention to detail, in-depth clinical and academic insights and evidenced knowledge of the history of violence and its roots in traumatic childhoods. Kahr continues to build on his previous work on forensic psychotherapy and to develop his own concepts and ideas such as the ‘infanticidal attachment’ (Kahr, 2007), ‘psychological infanticide’ (Kahr, 1993), forensic psychotherapy as a ‘psychological vaccine’ (Kahr, 2018a) and the ‘sub-clinical forensic perpetrator’ (Kahr, 2018b).

This book makes a significant contribution to forensic psychoanalysis. It delivers a systematic and comprehensive review of the history of forensic psychoanalysis and includes extensive historical research that traces the treatment of forensic patients across time (from the Babylonians to current times) and the application of psychoanalytic thinking to this specialist field, from Sigmund Freud to Estella Welldon and many other contemporary psychoanalysts. One of the most fascinating aspects of this book is the careful gathering of information and views from multiple sources and professionals, such as neuroscientists, psychiatrists, researchers, physicians and those involved with the application of the law.

Kahr is a prolific writer with an impressive record of books and articles to his name and an enviable capacity to draw his audience into complex and challenging subjects with ease and curiosity. His clinical vignettes are poignant and captivating. For those working with severely disturbed and disturbing children, adolescents and adults with a forensic presentation, his personal accounts of those moments of dread in the countertransference feel easy to identify with. The way he introduces and weaves his own thoughts and ideas into both the academic and the clinical material makes the style of his writing personable, hugely engaging and at times also moving. A number of clinical cases are of adolescents and young adults, making this book more pertinent to the thinking and work of child and adolescent psychoanalytic psychotherapists.

Twenty-three percent of children and young people in England have a long-term health condition (Brooks et al., 2015). As this current Research Digest will show there is a wealth of evidence for the psychological impact chronic physical conditions1 have within childhood. For example, King et al. (2024) report that at least one quarter of young people with a long-term health condition in England also have a probable mental health condition, compared with around 16% in the general population (NHS Digital, 2021, cited in King et al., 2024) and Brady et al. (2021), using data from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children2, found ‘children with chronic health problems presented with a disproportionate rate of psychiatric illness at 10 years, and these chronic health problems continued to be associated with poor mental health outcomes at 13 years and 15 years’ (p. 885). Unfortunately, it is often the case, ‘that children with physical and mental health conditions are viewed as complex; the care of their physical health may be prioritised, inadvertently leading to neglect of their mental health needs’ (Bennet et al. 2015, p. 308). It is therefore evident that this is a cohort of children and young people who require careful attention when considering their mental health needs. This is especially so as it is well documented that co-morbid psychiatric symptoms can negatively impact on the adherence to medical protocols and management of the physical health condition (de Araujo Filho & Yacubian, 2013) thus exacerbating the impact of the long-term health condition on their lives.

Rachel Acheson  

I write this editorial in October, in the midst of strong winds and heavy rain. I find myself continually looking out the window at the pouring rain, feeling regretful that my family will not be able to enjoy time outside this weekend, and worrying about old trees in my garden. The oft repeated refrain ‘where did the summer go?’ comes to mind, as for me, the rhythm of the seasons changing has felt sudden. The Journal also has its own kind of rhythm, although in a similar fashion I always feel surprised by the deadline for the December issue after the summer break. Inevitably, these rhythms are disrupted by frequent ‘storms’ which threaten to throw our well laid plans off course – papers are delayed, a last-minute issue emerges around consent, or our publishing software is glitching. Now in my fifth year at the Journal, I’ve learnt to anticipate, and indeed plan for this. What could be a storm, then becomes a minor tremor, and we recover our rhythm. This is possible, largely because the Journal is healthy – we are fully staffed, are generously supported by a large group of volunteer editors and peer reviewers, and receive a steady stream of high-quality new submissions (many from warmer climates than the UK!). We can weather many storms.

Rhythm, music and time are themes explored in some of the papers contained within this issue. Ansaldo explores in this issue’s first paper how, when working well, the dialogue between therapist and patient can have a musical quality. She is particularly concerned with how one develops the capacity to ‘play music’ in therapy, and how as teachers and supervisors we support its development:

To play music, a therapist needs to be able to find their own voice (Horne, 2023), while relinquishing the constraints of an excessively strict analytic stance … they need to be able to access a degree of internal freedom: an open and flexible psychic stance in the encounter with patients, leading to spontaneity and creativity in the therapeutic work.

Flavia Ansaldo

Flavia Ansaldo

37 Mapesbury Road, London NW2 4HJ, UK
Flavia.ansaldo@gmail.com

Flavia Ansaldo  

Child psychotherapy, psychoanalytic technique, analytic superego, transference object, developmental object, supervision

When it works well, the psychotherapeutic dialogue between therapist and patient can be creative, intuitive, ‘musical’. Drawing largely on Winnicott’s ideas, this paper describes the developmental process of ‘playing music’ as child psychotherapists, by describing what ‘musical’ inclinations look like in the psychotherapeutic work with patients, and how these inclinations can be fostered, in ourselves as well as in others (when in a teaching or supervisory role). Playing music in child psychotherapy has less to do with strictly adhering to psychoanalytic technique, and more to do with the therapist’s and patient’s ability to access internal freedom and creativity. In this paper, the author describes the internal and external dynamics that may facilitate or hinder the ‘musicality’ of child psychotherapists, focusing on the concept of the ‘analytic superego’ and issues of identity for today’s child psychotherapists. The author also acknowledges the complexity which derives from the increase in diversity in both psychoanalytic practitioners and patients, and the importance for the therapist to be a real object, as well as a transference object, by reflecting on and, where appropriate, addressing issues of sameness and difference in the therapeutic relationship.

Autistic adolescents who experience psychotic episodes present complex clinical challenges. Conventional therapeutic approaches may fall short in engaging with the symbolic disruptions and affective fragmentation seen in such presentations. This case study explores a psychodynamically oriented treatment of a 16-year-old autistic adolescent male following a substance-induced psychotic breakdown, framed through Lacanian and classical psychoanalytic concepts. The paper aims to illustrate how individualised symptom structures – particularly Lacan’s notion of the Sinthome —can be integrated into psychodynamic therapy to support stabilisation, emotional regulation, and symbolic expression. The case study demonstrates how a psychodynamically informed approach that respects and utilises the patient’s idiosyncratic organising mechanisms can foster symbolic integration, emotional containment, and therapeutic change. The Sinthome, far from being a barrier, can become an entry point into shared meaning-making when approached with clinical creativity and theoretical grounding.

Maria Eugenia Valdivia Rossel   Psychoanalytic child and adolescent psychotherapist working in CAMHS services within the NHS since 2017. She currently works in East London NHS Foundation Trust, in private practice at 10 Windsor Walk in London, and teaches on the Birkbeck MSc Psychodynamics of Human Development. The published study is part of her doctoral thesis. She trained at the Tavistock and Portman NHS Foundation Trust.
Silence, silent child, child and adolescent psychotherapy, infant observation, countertransference, interpretative phenomenological analysis

This study explores the experience of child psychotherapists who work with silent children. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with a purposive sample of four child and adolescent psychoanalytic psychotherapists and interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA) was used to examine the unique meaning that participants attributed to their work with their silent patients. Four superordinate themes emerged from the data: formulations of the silent child – ‘just different’; technique and cautious adaptation – ‘I needed to try something different’; the therapist’s feelings; and the tension between the need for support, and resistance to accessing it. This study aims to highlight the value of long-term work with silent children and strengthen understanding of the need for a mixed approach, which includes psychoanalytic technique and its cautious adaptation, to enliven the withdrawn child. The child psychotherapist’s skill of working with nonverbal communication based on infant observation and countertransference is central, but flexibility is also required.

Liz Bodycote

Liz Bodycote

London, UK
liz.bodycote@googlemail.com

Liz Bodycote   Studied economic and social history as an undergraduate before going on to train in social work at the end of the 1980’s. She worked in a number of roles within social welfare as a probation officer, child and family social worker and Children’s Guardian in the family courts before going on to train at the Tavistock Centre as a child and adolescent psychotherapist. After qualifying in 2011, she worked for 10 years in Newham CAMHS before retiring from the NHS. Since 2022 she has worked clinically at the Baobab Centre for Young Survivors in Exile. She is a member of the ACP Climate Emergency Group and a non-executive director on the ACP Board.
Climate breakdown, CAMHS, neoliberalism, Uncare, analytic hour

This paper proposes that the heritage derived from the ‘analytic hour’ offers a ‘technology’ which has a central place in thinking about the role of the psychoanalytic child and adolescent psychotherapist in relation to the climate and ecological emergency. It draws on associated disciplinary perspectives to consider the nature of ‘time’ in the climate of organisational working life, particularly as it has evolved within our public sector, and how the difficulty of working as a child psychotherapist in this context stems from some of the same roots as the climate crisis. In so doing, the paper explores the political economy in which this work is situated, namely the rise of neoliberalism, and seeks to make explicit the fundamental conflict between its founding assumptions with regard to human nature and those of psychoanalysis. Whilst suggesting that such ontological dissonance is at the heart of a climate breakdown experienced within the public work setting, it is proposed that psychoanalytic child psychotherapy is potentially a discipline for our times: with its realist theoretical foundation in tune with limits revealed in nature, it seeks to preserve a framework of time in which layers of depth might be apprehended with relational understandings at its core. It is thus in the technology of ‘holding the time’ that child psychotherapists can make a unique contribution to the rising generation, for whom we hold moral responsibilities as ancestors in the face of climate breakdown.

Birth order, primary schools, mental health, child psychotherapy, trauma-informed schools

Freud asserted that birth order should be considered in every life history assessment, yet birth order has been underinvestigated in the field of child psychotherapy and allied fields such as educational and developmental psychology. An overview of birth order research and accounts of birth order perspectives in child psychotherapy and psychoanalytic literature are considered. Data from consecutive referrals (n = 174, 60% males and 40% females) to two UK primary school counselling services (children aged 5–11) were collected with a view to understanding more about possible patterns in birth order among referrals. The data analysis revealed that the number of siblings in the families ranged from one to nine, with a mean of 4.4 siblings. Males were over-represented across all birth order categories (eldest, middle, only child and youngest). Youngest siblings (39%) and children from larger families (three to six children) were over-represented (78%). Singletons (only children) were under-represented (6%). The data points to the increased vulnerability of younger siblings from larger families, and the protective factors for females and only children. The findings have implications for counsellors and psychotherapists working in primary schools, and more generally practitioners working with children and young people who should become more accustomed to considering birth order when assessing risk and vulnerability. Understanding birth order might also be of value to professions allied to psychotherapy such as teachers who have the purview of the children in their class, who can assess risk factors and plan accordingly.

Anna Marrion  

Lucy Jones has struck a chord with the many who have read ‘Matrescence’ (longlisted for the Women’s Prize for Non-Fiction) for articulating what mother-becoming looks and importantly feels like at this moment in time, in WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic) countries. Encountering her own biases and lack of understanding about the emotional, physiological and political aspects of mothering inspired her to write the book, as did coming across anthropologist Dana Raphael’s term, ‘Matrescence’ (Raphael, 1975) shortly after giving birth. This offered her a narrative of her experience which, like adolescence, was developmental; that she was becoming a new version of herself, rather than failing.

The book is a compelling mix of intimate personal narrative and rigorous investigative journalism which unravels motherhood from the ribbons and bows of sentimentality and maternal ‘instinct’. Jones digs into every crevice of motherhood, illuminating the way with perspectives from evolutionary biology, sociology, anthropology, existential philosophy, ecology, neuroscience and psychoanalysis as well as a generous deep dive into her own body and mind. Her mission is to interrogate the mother-myths at the interface where patriarchy meets capitalism, arguing that these deny the importance of nurture and care, and exploit those who perform this labour.

Her chapter on birth is an exposé of the romanticism of the natural birth movement and its reliance on a Darwinian definition of women as ‘perfectly adapted’ for childbirth. She introduces the brilliantly pompously named, mid-century obstetrician, Grantly Dick-Read and his notion that culture and civilisation have conspired to create fear of childbirth in the ‘modern woman’, in contrast to the ‘primitive woman’ who simply ‘births in a thicket’. His prevailing theory (and Jones has scoured the research so we can be confident that it remains such) was that women experienced ‘Fear-Tension-Pain Syndrome’ and that pain in childbirth could be avoided if women would only relax, trust in their bodies and let nature take its course. Jones traces the echoes of Dick-Read’s ideas through to the feminist movement in the 1970s, the founding of the National (previously Natural) Childbirth Trust (NCT), and the language of prominent advocates of natural birth such as Sheila Kitzinger and Ina May Gaskin, demonstrating their evocation of birthing women as natural in the sense of timeless, enduring and revered, but never in the sense of, say, violent, or capricious or deathly.

Helen Ritzema  

The current Research Digest focuses on the impact of parental divorce, separation and interparental conflict on children and adolescents. Data shows parental divorce and separation form the experience for many young people within the UK today.

There were 2.4 million separated families in Great Britain and 3.8 million children in those separated families (Gov Statistics 2014 – 2023).

42% of marriages end in divorce (ONS, 2013a) Almost half of divorces involve children under 16 years (ONS, 2012).

27% of couples that were cohabiting when their child was born will have separated by the time the child is aged five. By contrast, 9% of couples that were married when their child was born will have separated by their child’s fifth birthday (Crawford, 2011).

Almost 25% of families in the UK are lone parent families (ONS, 2013b).

A search conducted into the reporting of parental divorce, separation and interparental conflict in clinical and theoretical papers within the Journal of child psychotherapy identified only two papers - Lohr et al. (1981) and Urwin (1998). In researching the topic, it was also noted that it is a subject area which often receives only the briefest mention within theoretical and clinical psychoanalytic books. This situation is striking, given that, clinically, the impact of parental divorce, separation and interparental conflict is undeniable.

Within the ‘Handbook of attachment’, Feeney et al.’s (2016) chapter entitled ‘Divorce through the lens of attachment theory’ describes the way in which parental divorce has the potential to reduce the ‘child’s confidence in who and where his or her attachment figures are; in his or her perceived acceptability in the eyes of attachment figures; and in the availability, accessibility, and sensitive responsiveness of attachment figures’ (p. 949). In their paper, published in 1981, Lohr et al. describe the way in which, the ‘loss of continuity in the parental relationship can serve as a “developmental interference”’ (p. 123). Co-Construction of a Common Language: From Shared Silence to Psychoanalytic Dialogue With a Patient on the Autism Spectrum

Chiara Cattelan

Chiara Cattelan

Venice, Italy

Chiara Cattelan   Training and supervising child and adult psychoanalyst at the Italian Psychoanalytic Society, where she served in the child/adolescent training programme from 2021 to 2024. She is a paediatrician and child psychiatrist and worked at the Paediatric Department of Padua University where she created a consultation and therapeutic unit for ASD children and their parents. Main interests include the early development of the mind, autistic states in children and adults, body-mind relationship. On these subjects, she has lectured and published articles and chapters in books. She works in private practice in Venice with adults, adolescents, and children.
Autism, space, mediation, cooperation, common language, subjectivation

This paper explores the challenge of constructing a common language between the analyst and a patient on the autistic spectrum. It describes the difficulties the patient encounters using words and exemplifies the process that leads to shared ways of communicating. It relies on clinical fragments from the work with a patient, now 18, who has been in psychoanalysis four times a week since age two and a half. At the beginning, there was no verbal communication or eye contact and no representation of space between self/other and between the patient’s sounds, which were long, apparently meaningless sequences, sought for the sensation they provided. Crossing the space between inside and outside triggered the anxiety of falling. Communication began with elementary forms of attunement. Shared experiences within the setting’s rhythmicity helped to transform the patient’s sense of intolerable emptiness into a representation of space within oneself and between oneself and the other. Out of a two-dimensional/adhesive situation, patient and analyst were able to create forms of mediation to cross space and adventure into the intangible dimension of imagination, granting at least partial access to abstract conceptions. The way the analyst listened to and addressed the patient as a subject as well as the patient’s role as a promoter was important in this transformation. The patient’s active role in co-constructing a common language led to a more cohesive self and the capacity to reflect on his own experience.

Peter Fonagy   Head of the Division of Psychology and Language Sciences at University College London; former Chief Executive of the Anna Freud Centre, UK; Consultant to the Child and Family Programme at Baylor College of Medicine and visiting professor at Yale and Harvard Medical Schools. He has received Lifetime Achievement Awards from several national and international professional associations.
Complex trauma, psychoanalytic psychotherapy, mentalization-based, parent work, network

Complex trauma involves severe and pervasive events such as abuse or profound neglect, in which there is usually a lack of a ‘safe haven’ for the young child, as their caregivers may be unavailable and/or a source of threat and danger. The impact of complex traumatic experiences on the child’s social, emotional and behavioural development is complex and pervasive, and burdens the mentalizing capacities of parents and other caregivers. In this paper, we propose a three-track approach to treat these children and their environment, in which direct psychotherapeutic work with the child goes hand in hand with a mentalization-based parent and network approach. In describing the case of Michael and his foster parents, we hope to show how complex trauma impacts the child’s development as well as the parents’ and network’s mentalizing capabilities, and illustrate what the three-track model can look like. We hope that our treatment guide can be of interest to child psychotherapists as well as to other mental health professionals, given the challenges of working with this group of children. In this regard, we have attempted to explain and frame relevant psychoanalytic concepts in concise and accessible language.

Catherine Webster   Psychoanalytic Child and Adolescent Psychotherapist. She completed her training with the Scottish Institute of Human Relations in 2013. Prior to her psychotherapy training she first worked as a drama and movement therapist and play specialist in London and later trained to be a play therapist. She moved to Edinburgh and worked as a freelance play therapist in primary schools and as a trainer for Children in Scotland. She has worked with children and adolescents for over 30 years and has also worked in family centres in Los Angeles, USA and Canberra, Australia. She now works for NHS Fife at Sea View, a CAMHS specialist sexual trauma project and also for the Infant Mental Health Team.
Sexual trauma, assessment, ambivalence, Pandora myth, shame and hope

This paper draws on the myth of Pandora and explores the metaphors within it to discuss the early stages of therapeutic work with children and young people who have suffered sexual abuse. The author underlines the importance of forming a professional network or team around the child, especially where developmental trauma is part of the child or young person’s experience. This contribution aims to show how the background history of the patient, like in the myth of Pandora, can be missed, and how gathering up the child or young person’s history is a key part of the early work. The author discusses how, for some patients, the idea of ‘opening up’ comes with a worry about being intruded into for fear of being overwhelmed by the trauma that they may have been working hard to defend against. Feelings of self-blame as well as deep-seated feelings of shame are often expressed by those who have suffered from sexual trauma in childhood and are present from early on in the work. The author discusses how blame is an undercurrent in the Pandora myth and how, on occasion within the clinical setting, this can be projected into the therapist. The author looks at the conundrum in the Pandora myth relating to the presence of hope: its potential in the recovery process but also its use as a defence. The paper concludes by considering the importance of hope, which is a key part of the myth and can act as a mobilising factor in the recovery of traumatised patients. The author outlines how the use of the ‘Hopes and expectations for treatment approach’ (HETA), devised by the child and adolescent psychotherapist Cathy Urwin might be used to capture and consider these issues at the end of the assessment period within the clinical setting.

Anna Freud, parent-toddler, parent–child relationship, adoption, early intervention, therapy group

This paper describes a long-running Anna Freudian approach to working therapeutically with toddlers and their parents in a group setting, developed and adapted by child psychotherapists working as part of the social enterprise, Chorus, to be delivered to adopted toddlers and their parents, soon after placement. The paper outlines the history of the Parent-Toddler Group (PTG) model and the adaptations made to develop this into Chorus’s Adoption Parent-Toddler Group (APTG), in partnership with Adopt London South. It then defines and describes four clinical concepts that have emerged as central to the intervention: Parental Authority, group approach, play and observation and developmental context. Finally, aspects of these concepts are illustrated through a composite case example.

Rapid onset gender dysphoria, adolescence, identity confusion, primitive defences, splitting, projection

This paper explores the complex psychological landscape of youth gender transition, focusing on the interplay between primitive defences against pain, parental influence, and identity formation. It addresses the difficult decisions parents face regarding the irreversible nature of medical interventions in the context of their children’s urgent desire for relief from psychological distress, particularly among young women experiencing rapid onset gender dysphoria (ROGD). The conflict between parental concerns about long-term consequences and the immediate needs of young individuals is critically examined, drawing on psychoanalytic theories, particularly Freud’s concepts of pleasure and reality principles. The analysis highlights the tension between a child’s yearning for autonomy and the potential psychological ramifications of premature medical transitions. Through this lens, it advocates for a careful, reflective approach that prioritises the young person’s emotional well-being while considering the long-term effects of medical interventions.

This charity provides psychotherapy for children, young people and their families. She specialises in working with autistic children and young people. She also leads an infant observation seminar at Exeter University. She has previously worked in CAMHS. She is a member of the Association of Child Psychotherapists.
Social media, adolescence, transitional space, attunement, attachment, parenting

This paper examines the impact of smartphone use on the developing personality. While holding in mind the potentially positive aspects of smartphone engagement, such as providing solace and support to marginalised groups, the paper focuses on the idea that excessive smartphone use by children and adolescents can impair development by providing a source of constant distraction, inhibiting the capacity to manage transitions and solitude, limiting offline creativity. Central to the paper is the understanding that adolescence heralds a period in which much of the infantile stage may be re-enacted or forged anew to support development. By juxtaposing the distance between an adolescent’s outstretched arm when posing for a selfie and the physical space between a parent and their babe in arms, the paper probes the underlying motivations behind excessive selfie-posting and considers the longer-term effect to the individual when most of this online feedback is based on filtered pictures that do not represent a realistic self. This paper also explores the effect of the increasing amount of time parents spend on digital devices: if, optimally, the infant builds a concept of self through their experience of what is reflected to them through their primary carer’s eyes, what is the consequence of the carer’s constant checking of their phone? The paper concludes by considering how mental health professionals might support parents to navigate the role of technology in their children’s lives.

Adolescent psychotherapy, symbolisation, containment, screen use, mentalization

This paper explores the psychodynamic treatment of Liam, a 14-year-old adolescent boy referred following a prolonged period of social withdrawal and immersive digital preoccupation. His relationship to his smartphone was not merely excessive – it had become essential to his psychic survival. Drawing on contemporary psychodynamic theories of digital objects, auxiliary ego functions, and symbolic collapse, the paper conceptualises Liam’s digital attachment as a transitional defence against internal fragmentation. Across the course of treatment, Liam’s compulsive digital retreat gave way to tentative forms of symbolic thought and relational presence. Rather than aiming to eliminate screen use, the therapy worked to create a containing space in which Liam’s digital defences could be interpreted, integrated, and eventually relinquished. Attention is given to the therapist’s role as a surviving object, the therapeutic function of digital mirroring, and the evolving transference within a world increasingly mediated by screens. The work suggests that for some adolescents, survival begins not with disconnection – but with symbolisation within and beyond the screen.

Hillel Mirvis   Senior Child & Adolescent Psychotherapist and Service Supervisor based at Dunstable CAMHS, having previously been in Barnet CAMHS (West) for 10 years, and is also in private practice. Hillel qualified at IPCAPA, where he leads clinical seminars on the child psychotherapy training, as well as acting as a progress advisor and intensive case supervisor. His various articles in the JCP have focussed largely on working with disturbed adolescents and with Looked After Children.
Technology, adolescence, exhibitionism, ‘acting out’

Adolescents’ use of technology has become an area of concern within multidisciplinary teams in the NHS, with broad consensus that it often facilitates further psychological deterioration in young people who are already vulnerable to mental health difficulties. The author wishes to promote a place for curiosity about the potential meaning, both conscious and unconscious, behind adolescents’ use of technology as they describe it to their therapists in the consulting room. It is suggested that there are unconscious reasons why individual adolescents are drawn towards specific websites or ‘apps’ in order to communicate their internal world, distress or wishes for change in their environment. Three composite cases are discussed in order to illustrate these points. It is suggested that child psychotherapists have a potentially important role to play in deepening understanding of these worrying developments in adolescents’ lives. It is also suggested that there may be unconscious barriers to our being able to think fully about these issues, which are explored further in the discussion.

Theodora Manolopoulou   Independent Child and Adolescent Psychoanalytic Psychotherapist. She completed her training at IPCAPA with the British Psychotherapy Foundation, Anna Freud Centre, and UCL. She specialises in psychotherapeutic interventions for adopted and looked-after children and earned her Doctorate in this field from UCL. After working in London Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) for more than 10 years, she set up a private practice in Northwest London. Dr Manolopoulou is currently part of a specialist team for children under five within London CAMHS. She leads a weekly Work Discussion Seminar for an MSc program at UCL/Anna Freud Centre where she is also a Visiting Lecturer. Dr Manolopoulou has pioneered and engaged in interdisciplinary projects that integrate psychoanalytic thinking with other fields such as architecture and music.
Screens, dependency, addiction, narcissism, technoference, under 5s

Mobile screens have infiltrated nearly all households worldwide. While significant attention has been given to the effects of mobile screens on adolescents, the impact on children under the age of five and their developing relationships with primary caregivers remains largely unexamined. This paper will address the themes of weaning and separation, drawing upon prominent psychoanalyst Margot Waddell’s work . It will explore how these concepts have evolved since the publication of her influential book ‘Inside lives’. Key concepts such as infantile omnipotence, dependency, continuity of being, narcissism, and the roles of third and transitional phenomena will be discussed. The defensive use of mobile screens by primary caregivers and the idea of using these screens as modern pacifiers will be explored. Fictionalised examples from settings for specialist under five services in Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) and the community will be presented. The aim is to explore how primitive feelings are evoked in children under five and their primary caregivers due to screen use and how maturation can be impeded. The potential dynamic role of child psychotherapists in addressing these issues in clinical settings by holding a thinking stance rather than a judgemental one will be discussed. Furthermore, the involvement of child psychotherapists in policy-making and working within interdisciplinary contexts will be explored.

Literature and the Therapeutic Imagination. Adoption, Charles Dickens and Psychoanalysis

Robert Fleming

Robert Fleming

rwkfleming@me.com

Robert Fleming   Child and Adolescent Psychotherapist and worked for the South London and Maudsley NHS Trust until retiring from the NHS and working with children, adolescents and adults in independent practice. He has a long standing interest in the dynamics of all involved in the adoption process. He teaches in many locations and supervises psychotherapists at various points in their careers.
Adoption, Dickens, literature, psychoanalysis, therapeutic imagination, training

This paper begins with the idea that English literature contains many explorations of the psychological processes of adoption. Although adoption is an intriguing narrative device, it could be argued that psychoanalysis adds further understanding of the deeper reasons for this. There is a long tradition of psychoanalysis being interested in literature and the paper traces the roots of this from Freud to more recent writers. A good exemplar of literature exploring adoption is found in many of the works of Charles Dickens such as David Copperfield, Great Expectations, Nicholas Nickleby and Oliver Twist. Although Bleak House is often regarded as being mainly about a dysfunctional legal system, the paper argues that it also contains a perceptive account of a child in the adoption process. Themes of ‘not knowing’, searching and re-unification, identity and the use of transitional objects are all present in this novel. Finally, the paper suggests that any clinicians working with the inner world could be enriched by paying close attention to the novelist’s imaginative exploration of the adoption process. This point is made through the consideration of the work of Jeremy Holmes. The therapeutic imagination could be enhanced by bringing the study of literature into the training and development of psychotherapists.
